moments.title: First Impressions drafted
moments.body: 1796-97: Austen, aged 20-21, drafts 'First Impressions' at Steventon. Her father offers it to a publisher (Thomas Cadell, London) who returns it unread. Austen revises substantially over the next 15 years before publication.
moments.takeaway: Austen's writing life is one of patient revision. Most of her novels exist in multiple drafts over decades.

moments.title: Pride and Prejudice published
moments.who: Austen, 'by the author of Sense and Sensibility'
moments.body: 28 January 1813: Pride and Prejudice published in three volumes by Egerton. 1,500 copies. Sold out quickly. Austen sold the copyright outright for £110. The novel is published anonymously — 'By the Author of Sense and Sensibility'.

quote.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
quote.attrib: Jane Austen, opening of Pride and Prejudice, 1813

moments.takeaway: Austen made roughly £670 from her writing in her lifetime — modest, but more than she could have made in any other respectable way.

moments.title: Austen dies
moments.body: 18 July 1817: Austen dies, probably of Addison's disease. Her brother Henry's biographical notice attached to Northanger Abbey (1818) revealed her identity. The novels remained in print throughout the 19th century but her reputation grew dramatically in the 20th.
moments.takeaway: Modern Austen scholarship — Mary Lascelles's pioneering work, the Cambridge editions, biographers — has built her into one of the central English novelists.

now.title: Austen in mass culture
now.body: Andrew Davies's 1995 BBC adaptation (Colin Firth in a wet shirt) launched a generation of adaptations. Bridget Jones (1996), film versions (1940, 2005), Bollywood (Bride and Prejudice 2004) and continuous reworkings. Janeites — fans devoted to her work — sustained interest from the 1890s onwards.
now.open_questions: Was Austen a conservative or a radical? Most modern critics see her as conservatively-liberal — within the gentry world but acute about its absurdities. The marriage plots are both fairy tales and economic analyses.

reflection: A clergyman's daughter living in Hampshire wrote six novels that remade the English novel. Her irony, her psychological precision and her free indirect discourse shaped the form for two centuries — and her plots still satisfy.
